title: Stocks Enter Correction as AI Sell-Off Wipes Out the Nasdaq's 2026 Gains

content:
Wall Street's worst stretch of the year deepened Friday, pushing the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average into correction territory as an artificial-intelligence sell-off wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the entire year.

The S&P 500 fell 3.70% on Friday, Nov. 20, closing at 6,910.39 — its seventh consecutive losing session, its longest losing streak since February 2020, and more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record. The Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, also more than 10% below its recent peak. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.28% to 22,617.73, erasing every gain it had made in 2026.

For the week, the S&P 500 lost 8.6%, its worst week since April 2025; the Dow fell 8%, its worst week since March 2020; and the Nasdaq dropped about 10%.

The selling centered on Nvidia, the bellwether of the AI boom. The chipmaker plunged about 14% on Friday to $125.53 after Reuters reported that U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are examining the company's accounting practices. Neither the SEC nor the company commented on the report, and an inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing. Nvidia fell 22.9% for the week — its worst week since October 2008 — erasing roughly $500 billion in market value in a single session. AMD fell more than 13% and Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.

Anthropic, which made a record stock-market debut Thursday, fell 8.5% on its second day of trading. The market's fear gauge, the VIX, spiked toward 36, its highest level since April 2025.

What it means here

The indexes at the center of the sell-off are the same ones tracked by the retirement and investment funds many Webb County families hold. A correction — a drop of 10% or more from a recent peak — does not by itself say where markets go next, and Friday's losses came after the indexes set records only weeks ago.

Nvidia's slide also follows a leadership shake-up: co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on Nov. 12, and chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO.
